title: Gold holds near $3,930 as Iran talks, U.S. midterms shape outlook
full_text:
Investing.com -- Gold prices held near $3,930 an ounce on Tuesday as investors monitored fresh diplomatic efforts to resolve the U.S.-Iran conflict and awaited U.S. midterm election results for clues on the outlook for interest rates and fiscal policy.
At 19:54 ET (00:54 GMT), spot gold fell marginally to $3,927.87 an ounce, while U.S. gold futures declined 0.1% to $3,936.50.
Silver slipped 0.4% to $49.5750 an ounce, while platinum rose 0.2% to $1,421.51. Spot palladium gained 0.1% to $937.60, while palladium futures were little changed at $930.50. The U.S. dollar Index fell 0.2% to 101.70.
Bullion eased modestly after gaining nearly 2% in the previous session, leaving prices volatile this week as conflicting signals on U.S.-Iran negotiations complicated the inflation outlook.
Oil prices fluctuated within a range of around $5 a barrel on Tuesday as Washington and Tehran reviewed new proposals from mediators aimed at resolving their differences and preventing a return to full-scale conflict, according to reports.
The diplomatic developments followed limited U.S. airstrikes on targets on Iran's Qeshm Island within the Strait of Hormuz the previous night. Oil had surged over the past month as regional tensions intensified but reversed sharply this week after signs that the White House was prepared to give negotiations more time.
Crude and gold have generally moved in opposite directions recently, as elevated energy prices fuel inflation and increase expectations of higher interest rates, weighing on non-yielding bullion.
Gold fell almost 7% in October, breaking below the $4,000-an-ounce threshold at the end of the month after investors retreated from artificial intelligence-related investments and sold bullion to cover losses elsewhere.
The metal has also declined around 25% since the U.S.-Iran conflict erupted in late February, as accelerating inflation prompted tighter monetary policy.
Investors are now watching Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, which will determine control of both the House of Representatives and Senate.
The outcome could reshape expectations for U.S. fiscal policy and indirectly influence gold demand as traders assess the implications for government deficits, inflation and monetary policy.

title: James Talarico becomes first Democrat to win statewide in Texas since 1994
full_text:
By Nolan D. McCaskill
Nov 3 (Reuters) - State Representative James Talarico won the US Senate race in Texas on Tuesday, according to media projections, defeating President Donald Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton to end Democrats’ 32-year statewide losing streak and give his party a major boost in the battle for Senate control.
It was a striking Democratic breakthrough in a state Republicans have long dominated. Trump carried the state by 14 percentage points in 2024. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, has been at the center of controversies that include a 2023 impeachment and a securities fraud case.
Talarico, a four-term state legislator and one of the nation’s top Senate fundraisers, overcame heavy outside spending in the most expensive Senate race of the cycle. He began as an underdog against former US Representative Colin Allred, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee, who later withdrew to run for Congress again.
Talarico went on to defeat US Representative Jasmine Crockett for the Democratic nomination, dealing a political blow to his former state legislative colleague.
Republicans spent more than $316 million to retain the seat. Republican US Senator John Cornyn was ousted in a primary runoff after Trump endorsed Paxton. Republican leaders had viewed Cornyn as the stronger general-election candidate.
Paxton used his role as attorney general to sue former President Joe Biden’s administration more than 100 times.
Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday’s elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.

title: Marubeni H1 profit jumps 45% on commodities, trading; hikes annual guidance
full_text:
Investing.com-- Marubeni Corp. (TYO:8002) clocked strong earnings for the six months to September 30, with the Japanese trading house hiking its annual guidance on strength in its commodities and trading units.
Marubeni said adjusted net profit– which excludes one-off items– rose 45% year-on-year to 318.0 billion yen ($2.02 billion).
The trading house, which is part of Japan’s big five “sogo shosha,” benefited from surging metal prices, which boosted returns from its mining and smelting operations, while also bringing big returns for its trading businesses.
Non-resources profit– which stems from Marubeni’s chemicals, trading, lifestyle, and agricultural holdings– also firmed sharply in the period.
Revenue rose 23% to 5.180 trillion yen, while non-adjusted net profit rose 11% to a record high of 338.0 billion yen.
The trading house hiked its outlook for the year across the board. Net profit is now expected at a record-high 630 billion yen, up from prior expectations of 580 billion yen.
Adjusted net profit is expected at a record-high 600 billion yen, up from prior forecasts of 540 billion yen. Surging commodity prices are expected to be among the biggest earnings drivers for the company.
Still, shares of the trading house fell 3% to 4,676 yen after the print.

title: Democrats flip US Representative Tom Kean’s New Jersey district
full_text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrat Rebecca Bennett defeated US Representative Tom Kean of New Jersey on Tuesday, according to US media, flipping a Republican-held seat.
Bennett is a former US Navy helicopter pilot.
Kean was the most vulnerable Republican in New Jersey’s congressional delegation. He flipped the Democratic-held seat in 2022 but disappeared from the public for months in an election year before disclosing this summer his battle with depression.
President Donald Trump carried the district by 1.2 percentage points in 2024.
Nationally, Democrats need to net four seats to win control of the US House of Representatives.

title: Top takeaways from the US midterm elections
full_text:
By Tim Reid and Trevor Hunnicutt
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Americans went to the polls on Tuesday in midterm elections that will determine who controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s term.
Here are some takeaways from the elections.
A BLUE WAVE
Opinion polls ahead of the midterms showed a significant chance of a strong Democratic night, with the party favored to reclaim the US House and competing for control of the Senate.
But the scale of the Democratic gains suggested something larger: a potential blue wave that was extending well beyond the traditional battlegrounds and deep into Republican territory.
In Texas, James Talarico routed Republican Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat senator-elect in 38 years. Democrats have been dreaming of turning the Lone Star blue for decades.
In flipping the Senate seat in South Carolina, the party also made history. Democrats have not won a US Senate race in South Carolina this century, and the win by Annie Andrews over Republican Senator Darline Graham became another defining upset of the night.
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown prevailed, while in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton easily defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. Democrats last won a Senate seat in Kansas in 1932, during the Great Depression.
Democrats were projected by US media outlets to win back control of both the US House and the Senate.
Winning back Congress could be a double-edged sword for Democrats, however.
Voters likely will look to Democrats to address their economic concerns and not just oppose Trump. But they will be limited in what legislation they can pass as the president retains veto power. Trump could also say Democrats are now at the very least equally culpable for the state of the economy.
Trump told The New York Times he would accept the election results and was prepared to work with Democrats.
AN ANGRY ELECTORATE
Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot. They did, and Republicans paid the price on Tuesday.
Early results and exit polls showed an electorate in a sour mood, delivering a strong rebuke of Trump and his agenda as voters expressed deep unhappiness about high prices and the direction of the country.
Many said they feel worse off than two years ago and nearly 9 in 10 identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets that included major television networks and the Associated Press.
Trump was elected in 2024 on a promise to arrest high inflation, but his tariffs on foreign goods and war against Iran have only worsened the economic situation for many Americans. His response on the campaign trail was to tell Americans to absorb the higher costs even as his popularity sank to record lows.
Nearly two-thirds of voters in the exit polls blamed Trump for high prices, while three-quarters said they were either angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country. Voters also expressed widespread concern over government corruption.
Democratic victories on Tuesday suggested Trump’s 19-state campaign blitz for Republican candidates in recent weeks had done little to improve his standing with voters.
REJECTING TRUMP’S PICKS
It wasn’t just a bad night for Republicans; it was a bad night for Trump’s judgment. He suffered a series of personal defeats as several candidates he had elevated over the objections of local Republicans struggled in races the party had expected to win.
Trump’s handpicked Senate candidates in South Carolina and North Carolina, Graham and Michael Whatley, lost their races, while Paxton in Texas was soundly beaten. Trump’s choices left Republicans fighting on the defensive in states where they had been favored to win.
The losses are likely to revive questions about Trump’s political instincts, particularly his tendency to prioritize personal loyalty over candidates with broader electoral appeal.
The exit polls showed that the coalition of voters that powered his 2024 victory is badly fractured. Republicans recorded sharp declines in support among Black men, Latinos and young voters.
ECONOMY TRUMPS FEAR
In the closing weeks of the campaign, and lacking a coherent economic message, Trump and his fellow Republicans tried to paint Democrats as dangerous radicals and communists who would destroy the country if elected.
The scare tactics didn’t work. Voters were far more focused on the price of groceries and gas and wanted to hear more from Trump about how he would lower costs.
During the summer, Trump repeatedly argued that if Democrats won, "it’s going to be a communist country." He said Democratic establishments in various states had been replaced by "crazed lunatics and radicals."
Fear has often worked as a tactic in US elections, but in the end, Trump could not persuade voters that Democrats, one of the country’s two main political parties, really posed an existential threat to the United States.

title: Palantir shares retreat despite U.S. commercial sales spike
full_text:
Investing.com - Palantir shares slumped by more than 5% at the open of U.S. trading on Tuesday, dragged down by a soft indicator of future revenue that overshadowed otherwise solid third-quarter results.
The artificial intelligence-focused data analytics group logged earnings per share of $0.44, driven by a 96% surge in sales to $2.31 billion that was powered by robust commercial and government contracts in the United States. The two numbers -- along with a fourth-quarter outlook for sales of $2.649 billion-$2.653 billion and operating income of $1.64 billion-$1.644 billion -- outpaced estimates. Free cash flow also ticked up to $1.196 billion.
For the full year, the company raised its revenue forecast to between $8.53 billion and $8.534 billion, implying annual growth of approximately 91%. It also increased its U.S. commercial revenue growth forecast to at least 143%, with revenue expected to exceed $3.56 billion.
U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148% versus a year ago to $984 million, up 29% from the previous quarter and exceeding U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in the company’s history. Government revenue rose 96% year-over-year. Companies have been accelerating investments in AI as they race to integrate the technology into operational workflows.
Chief Executive Alex Karp said the growing adoption of what he called sovereign AI was creating a widening divide between institutions capable of deploying the technology and those falling behind.
Still, analysts flagged that growth in total contract value -- a tracker of the total dollar amount of all contracts signed during the quarter that helps shed light on possible incoming sales -- slowed to 6% versus a year ago. In the second quarter, the figure stood at 49%.
"[T]he headline income/cash flow statement figures are great (healthy beat-and-raise on revenue/operating income with very strong cash flow) but in the glass-half-empty mindset that tech finds itself in, people may walk away fairly neutral (or even modestly underwhelmed given some of the TCV details)," analysts at Vital Knowledge said in a note.
AI-exposed stocks have gyrated in recent weeks, driven by worries around the sustainability of large debt- and equity-fueled spending a rapid build-out of critical AI infrastructure like data centers and chips.
(Jaiveer Shekhawat contributed reporting)

title: Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state
full_text:
By Kat Stafford
Nov 3 - Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won Georgia’s race for governor on Tuesday, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US state and delivering Democrats a victory in one of the nation’s most closely divided political battlegrounds.
The former Atlanta mayor, who will also be the first female governor of the state, defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson, according to US media projections.
She succeeds Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who is leaving office after serving two consecutive terms. Bottoms, 56, also previously served as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement.
The victory marked a new milestone for Black women in American politics, who have long been a core base within the Democratic Party but remain underrepresented in the nation’s highest elected offices. The same evening, Stacey Plaskett was elected governor of the US Virgin Islands, a US territory, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US jurisdiction.
In Florida, Republican US Representative Byron Donalds was elected governor. Donalds is the first Black Republican to be elected governor in the US.
Bottoms’ win also marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground.
Republicans had controlled the governor’s office for more than two decades.
Jackson, the billionaire founder of healthcare staffing company Jackson Healthcare, cast himself as a political outsider and campaigned on tax cuts, public safety and reducing government regulation.
Bottoms’ victory comes eight years after fellow Democrat Stacey Abrams became the first Black woman nominated for governor by a major US political party.
Abrams lost governor’s races in Georgia in 2018 and 2022, but her campaigns helped to build a multigenerational, multiracial coalition that boosted Democratic turnout, helped elect two Democratic US senators and delivered Georgia’s electoral votes to a Democratic presidential candidate for the first time in decades.

title: Democrats seize Congress; AMD shares surge - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock averages point higher, as investors assess the impact of a major Democratic victory in the American midterm elections. A large wave of support for Democrats leaves the party set to take control of both chambers of Congress and markets pondering a potential move to decelerate the artificial intelligence build-out. Shares of Advanced Micro Devices surge in extended hours trading on an upbeat outlook powered by strong sales of data-center chips.
1. Futures climb
U.S. stock futures rose on Wednesday. By 03:37 ET (08:37 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had gained 15 points, or 0.2%, Nasdaq 100 futures had jumped by 64 points, or 0.2%, and Dow futures had climbed by 237 points, or 0.5%.
In the prior session, the benchmark S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite finished higher, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average declined. Optimism around a potential diplomatic solution to the Iran war helped to drive down oil prices and push up stocks, although significant uncertainty still surrounds the outlook for the Middle East conflict.
"That backdrop helped US equities to finally stage a recovery" from a recent retreat spurred by worries over the sustainability of massive debt-fueled expenditures on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Meanwhile, a new batch of data pointed to ongoing strength in the U.S. economy. For example, one tracker showed a jump in job openings to a four-month high, while a separate gauge of factory orders grew by more than anticipated.
2. Democrats seize Congress
Traders were now parsing through the long-awaited U.S. midterms, which saw Democrats secure control over both chambers of Congress.
A wave of backing for Democrats had been suggested by polls in the run-up to the election, as voters expressed frustration with affordability challenges and the Iran war. But that support for the party appears to have been even stronger than anticipated, with Democrats sweeping to victory in some statewide races in traditional strongholds of President Donald Trump's Republicans.
Crucially, the Democrats will hold majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate when Congress convenes in January, meaning that any new laws must require at least a modicum of Democratic approval. Still, Trump retains a critical veto power over legislation, granting the White House the ability to reject bills passed by both the House and Senate.
For markets, expectations have risen that the Democrats could use their Congressional control to place more stringent regulations on AI and slow the build-out of the nascent technology. AI was another key issue for American voters, particularly fears of possible job losses and discontentment with the proliferation of huge data centers.
Overnight, concerns over a decelerating AI rollout temporarily weighed on tech stocks in Asia and U.S. equity futures -- but those losses were later broadly pared back.
"Given AI's role in powering the U.S. economy, speculation over whether a new Democrat Congress would slow AI capex plans briefly hit markets," analysts at ING said in a note. "That the initial market moves are being reversed probably owes to the fact that the Democrats do not take office until January."
3. AMD dented by $1 billion in chip deal charges
Beyond politics, shares of Advanced Micro Devices surged by more than 7% in extended hours trading.
Soaring data-center sales led the AI chipmaker to unveiled 2027 growth that was faster than projected, sparking a after-hours rally in peers like Nvidia, Intel and Broadcom.
In a call with analysts, AMD CEO Lisa Su said overall revenue is now anticipated to expand by over 80% in 2027. According to data cited by Reuters, analysts had been expecting a forecast for growth of 77%.
Su noted that 80% of overall sales will come from chips designed for data centers, adding that these processors will "drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth."
However, AMD's third-quarter profits were hit by a more than $1 billion non-cash charge related to the firm's strategy of offering warrants to buy future stakes in the business to ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and Instagram-parent Meta Platforms. In return, these companies have committed to buy AMD chips.
More corporate earnings are due out on Wednesday, including returns from chip designer Arm Holdings and semiconductor name Qualcomm.
4. U.S. services activity data ahead
On the economic data front, a new reading of activity in the all-important U.S. services sector will be in focus.
The Institute for Supply Management's non-manufacturing purchasing managers' price index is seen edging down marginally to 54.8 in October, compared to 54.9 in the preceding month.
A level above 50 indicates expansion in the services industry, which accounts for over two-thirds of total U.S. economic activity.
Earlier this week, an ISM gauge of U.S. manufacturing activity increased thanks to solid domestic demand, although factory gate prices stayed elevated, underscoring ongoing inflationary pressures facing the industry.
5. Oil rises amid Iran uncertainty, Democrat triumph
Oil prices edged higher on Wednesday. As of 01:57 ET (06:57 GMT), Brent Oil Futures expiring in January rose 0.6% to $104.20 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained 0.5% to $96.59 per barrel.
The U.S. midterm election outcome could complicate the Trump administration’s policy agenda during a time when uncertainty surround whether the White House will pursue renewed military action against Iran or seek a diplomatic resolution.
Trump’s conflicting signals have added to this murky backdrop. The United States carried out what officials described as defensive strikes against Iranian air defense installations on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, earlier this week. title: Siltronic shares jump 8% as Q3 results beat estimates, 2026 outlook raised
full_text:
Investing.com -- Shares in Siltronic jumped more than 8% on Wednesday after the German wafer manufacturer reported third-quarter results above expectations and raised its full-year 2026 guidance, citing stronger wafer demand and favourable foreign exchange rates.
Third-quarter sales rose 18.3% year on year to €355.4 million, up 10.5% from the previous quarter and 6% above the company-compiled consensus of €335 million.

Net debt improved to €619.9 million from €836.5 million in fiscal 2025, supported by a capital increase. The equity ratio stood at 44.7%, up from 42.6% in the prior fiscal year. Net cash flow for the quarter was €57.6 million, compared to negative €27 million in the second quarter.

title: BMW cuts 2026 auto margin outlook to break-even; keeps cash flow target
full_text:
Investing.com -- BMW (ETR:BMWG) on Wednesday cut its 2026 profit forecast for its car business to break-even but kept its cash flow target, even as weak China sales and tariffs weigh.
The German carmaker now expects an automotive operating profit margin of -0.5% to 0.5% for 2026, down from a previous forecast of 1% to 3%, citing an expansion of portfolio and structural measures.
Forecast return on capital employed, which measures profit against money tied up in the business, fell to between -1% and 1% from 1% to 5%.
BMW said the total hit to the automotive margin this year is now around 2.5 percentage points, compared with 1.25 points previously.
It also pointed to currency effects, raw materials, price and product measures aimed at stabilising transaction prices in China and lower revenue from pre-owned vehicles as negative factors for 2026 earnings.
BMW maintained its forecast for automotive free cash flow of above €2.50 billion for 2026.
Free cash flow was €724 million in the first nine months, versus €2.69 billion a year earlier, as lower operating cash inflow, higher inventory build-up, lower provisions and lower earnings weighed.
In the third quarter it was -€566 million, versus €343 million a year earlier and an average estimate of €216 million.
Third-quarter pretax profit fell 10.6% to €2.08 billion from €2.33 billion a year earlier, below the €2.09 billion average estimate of nine analysts.
Pretax profit included a financial result of €494 million versus €68 million a year earlier, driven primarily by positive valuation effects from interest rate hedging transactions.
Group operating profit fell 29.7% to €1.59 billion from €2.26 billion, below the €1.71 billion estimate.
The automotive operating margin was 3.4% versus 5.2% a year earlier and an estimate of 3.1%, as negative market developments in China, higher depreciation and amortisation and negative currency effects weighed, partly offset by cost savings.
A settlement in the legal dispute over the Integrated Braking System also lowered cost of sales.
Deliveries fell 6.3% to 551,075 vehicles, against an average estimate of 550,056. In China, deliveries fell 24.8% to 114,445 as the overall market there shrank 24.6% after subsidy cuts for new-energy vehicles and subdued consumer demand. Deliveries rose 2.6% in Europe and 2.5% in the United States.
Additional U.S. tariffs cut the automotive margin by around 1.25 percentage points in the quarter, versus around 1.75 points a year earlier. BMW expects an impact of around 1.25 points for 2026, versus around 1.5 points in 2025.
BMW now expects deliveries to decline moderately in 2026, rather than slightly, and group pretax profit to fall significantly from €10.24 billion in 2025.

title: Pandora shares jump  7% as Q3 sales beat, tariff refund boosts profit
full_text:
Investing.com -- Shares in Danish jeweller Pandora jumped more than 7% on Wednesday after third-quarter like-for-like sales growth beat even the highest analyst estimate, although a one-off U.S. tariff refund accounted for more than the operating profit beat and sales growth slowed to 1% in October.
Like-for-like sales rose 4% in the quarter, beating the 2% analyst consensus and the highest estimate of 3%. Organic growth was 6%, against expectations of 4%, while revenue of DKK 6.69 billion exceeded the DKK 6.58 billion consensus.
Japan accounted for nearly half of the group’s like-for-like growth, although Pandora expects growth in the market to moderate.
Operating profit was DKK 1.06 billion, compared with the DKK 860 million consensus. This included DKK 246 million in one-off income from a partial refund of U.S. tariffs paid earlier, which boosted the operating margin by 370 basis points and the gross margin by 340 basis points.
The operating margin rose to 15.9% from 14.0% a year earlier, although Pandora said the underlying margin was broadly flat. The gross margin was 83.7%, above the 80.3% consensus, but would have been 80.3% excluding the tariff refund.
Earnings per share rose to DKK 6.9 from DKK 6.3 a year earlier, beating the DKK 5.8 consensus. Excluding the tariff refund and related financing costs and tax, earnings per share would have been DKK 5.0, down 20% from a year earlier, Pandora said.
Like-for-like sales growth slowed to 1% in October, which the company attributed to lower promotional activity. Underlying growth was around 3%, it said. The fourth quarter is historically a stronger period for revenue and profit.
Pandora narrowed its 2026 organic growth forecast to 2% to 3% from 0% to 3%, and its operating margin outlook to 22.5% to 23% from 22% to 23%. The margin revision primarily reflects a larger expected gain from the tariff refund, now forecast to add 130 basis points compared with 100 basis points previously.
The company also narrowed its full-year like-for-like growth forecast to 0% to 1% from -2% to 1%.
It raised its forecast for 2026 net financial expenses to DKK 1.20 billion to DKK 1.25 billion from DKK 1.10 billion to DKK 1.15 billion, citing foreign exchange and hedging losses.
For 2027, Pandora set an operating margin target of 14% to 15%, or 15.5% to 16.5% excluding one-off items, compared with previous targets of above 12% and above 14%, respectively.
The company said it had hedged 90% to 100% of its expected 2027 silver requirements at around $62 an ounce, compared with the $82 an ounce assumption used previously. Analyst consensus for its 2027 operating margin is 16.1%.
Free cash flow including lease payments was negative DKK 557 million, compared with positive DKK 218 million a year earlier. Inventories rose to 22.0% of revenue from 16.4%, reflecting higher metal prices, the switch to platinum plating and increased unit volumes, Pandora said.

The blue sweep was largely anticipated in opinion polls leading up the elections, which showed increasing voter discontent with President Donald Trump and the Republicans’ handling of high fuel prices, increased government corruption, and a prolonged war in Iran.
But a Democratic sweep of Congress likely brings more regulatory hurdles for crypto, given that the pro-crypto legislation passed in the first two years of Trump’s term were all largely Republican-backed.
The Democrats have maintained a largely skeptical stance towards crypto, and were also seen blocking key legislation for the industry, like the Clarity Act.
Trump will now have to contend with a Congress that is stacked against him for the next two years. While the president may resort to executive policy to bypass Congress, such policies are subject to changing between administrations.

title: Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate
full_text:
By Nathan Layne
DETROIT, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open US Senate seat on Tuesday, according to media projections, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber while preserving a crucial Democratic seat in the party’s fight for Senate control.
El-Sayed’s victory in the closely contested election marked a breakthrough for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing and denied Republicans a chance to flip the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.
El-Sayed, 42, a former public health official, focused on lowering costs for working families and reducing corporate influence in politics. His platform included Medicare for All, a government-funded universal healthcare program championed by progressives in his party.
Republicans held a 53-47 Senate majority going into Tuesday’s midterm elections, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats to take control.
His opponent Mike Rogers, 63, a former congressman and FBI agent, entered the race with strong backing from Trump and national Republicans and had sought to cast El-Sayed as a radical candidate sympathetic to Islamic extremism through alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims that El-Sayed denies and that remain unsupported by evidence. Democrats said the attacks on El-Sayed relied on Islamophobic tropes.
Rogers also devoted significant effort to courting Jewish voters who may have been uneasy with El-Sayed’s opposition to US military aid for Israel and his characterization of Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide.
But Rogers struggled to overcome voter concerns about the economy and Trump’s low ratings. In the closing weeks of the race, he broke with the president on the war in Iran and the US trade dispute with Canada, arguing that ending both was necessary to help bring down costs for businesses and consumers.
